newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Philippine maids discard mops to greet HK handover.
newsitem.headline: Philippine maids discard mops to greet HK handover.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Philippine maids in Hong Kong dumped dusters and brooms and wore their Sunday best for a two-day party to celebrate the territory's handover to China.

In a lively mixture of religion, music, national costumes, beauty pageants and sports competitions, Filipinas in colourful dress sang full-throated love ballads and danced to greet the transition of power at midnight on Monday.
Philippines First lady Amelita Ramos topped the bill to play piano at an "Extravaganza" on Sunday for up to 100,000 Filipinas over the two days.

"We're the biggest expatriate community," said Lorna Villanueva, a spokeswoman for Hong Kong's Bayanihan Trust, which helped organise the commemoration of the territory's return to China after more than 150 years of British rule.
In keeping with a devout Catholicism, the Philippines' event started with a celebration of Mass where the clerical habits of priests and nuns could be seen dotted throughout the crowd.
Being biggest does not confer any muscle in this booming city state where money is king, and maids, or "domestic helpers" as they are known here, are among the territory's lowest paid.
Many Filipinas are seeking to follow the example of their Hong Kong employers, renowned for their business acumen.
While many partied, hundreds of others queued at a booth for forms for the Open University of the Philippines.
One of the most popular courses is "entrepreneurial" skills, which many domestic helpers hope will help them escape their HK$4,000 (US$513) a month salaries in Hong Kong.
"I think it's very helpful to all of us, especially if you are going back to the Philippines," said Catarina Jonson, 46. "We want to be entrepreneurs," she said.
Many of Hong Kong's Philippine domestic helper population are skilled, but sought work in the territory because they could not find suitable employment in their own country.
Their remittances are a valuable injection into the Philippines' economy, where thousands of families rely on the millions of Hong Kong dollars flowing back each month.

Many are cautious despite Chinese President Jiang Zemin's promise to Philippine President Fidel Ramos of no rule changes for Philippine domestic helpers after July 1. Ramos said on Sunday he was confident the welfare of an estimated 150,000 Philippine workers here "will remain protected".
"I'm kind of apprehensive because the Chinese are communists," said Lisa, 26, a qualified secondary school teacher working as a maid in Hong Kong to support relatives at home.
Father Frank Pidgeon, a Redemptorist priest in Asia for almost three decades, said the maids would cope with whatever the world threw at them after July 1.
"They feel in a typically Filipino way: namely, what comes what comes," said Pidgeon, publisher of a newsletter in English and Tagalog.
"If anything happens, they are flexible. They're like the bamboo. "They can move and cope with any kind of situation."
